sections.body:
A **shared account** is what two people agree happened: the handover on Tuesday, the message that was sent, the money that went missing. Gaslighting is the repeated rewriting of that account, so that the person who was there begins to doubt their own memory and their own perception. The rewriting is the work. The doubt is the result.

Gaslighting is not an argument, and it is not a person who is wrong. A colleague who misremembers a date is wrong; a partner who is unfair is unfair; a friend who bends a sentence is careless. None of that rewrites the account, and none of it needs the word. A **gaslighter** is the person who does the rewriting: the one who denies the account and then attacks the person who holds it. The word names an act. It does not name a character, and it does not tell you what the person will do next.

The line that matters is between a denial that comes from carelessness and a denial that comes from a decision. A careless denial is said once, and it gives way when the other person shows the message or the receipt. A deliberate attack stays flat: the account is denied after the evidence appears, and the person who holds it is then treated as the problem. The second kind is the one this article is about, and it is a pattern over time rather than a single hard sentence.

There is no test that tells you whether a person is gaslighting you, and nothing here gives you one. People disagree about how common the pattern is, and about how many remarks make a pattern out of separate remarks. Where the answers differ, the safest reading is to watch what the words do to the shared account: if the account stops moving with the evidence, something is wrong with the conversation, whatever it is called.
examples: The account was rewritten, and the person who was there began to doubt it.
A careless denial gives way when the message is shown; a deliberate attack stays flat.
The word names an act, not a character.
sections.heading: What gaslighting is, and what it is not

terms.example: It was gaslighting: the account of the meeting was rewritten until she doubted what she had heard.
terms.gloss: The repeated rewriting of a shared account of events, so that the person who was there begins to doubt their own memory.

terms.example: The gaslighter kept the denial flat and turned the talk to her character.
terms.gloss: The person who denies the shared account and attacks the person who holds it; the word names the act, not the character.

terms.example: Their shared account of the shift was simple, and both of them could still say it.
terms.gloss: What two people agree happened, and what each of them remembers about it.

sections.body:
The first move is the flat denial: *that never happened*, *I never said that*, *you are misremembering*. The sentence is short, and it is said in the same tone every time, so it starts to sound like a fact about the world and not like a claim about it. The evidence does not change the sentence. A message that answers the message is the hardest thing to deny, so that is usually the one denied hardest.

The second move is to redefine the words. *Aggressive* becomes *you are being loud*. *Late* becomes *you were never on time*. *Rude* becomes *you are sensitive*. The word in the room and the word in the message are no longer the same word, and the reader is left defending a version of the conversation that nobody had. This is **revisionism**: the account is kept, but its terms are changed until the meaning that was shared is gone.

The third move is to change the subject, not by refusing to answer but by answering a different question. *What about what you did last week?* The new subject is louder, and it is not the subject of the account, so the account is never settled. Where the money went is replaced by a complaint about the person's tone, and the question about the money is left standing as though it had never been asked. This is **deflection**: the answer moves away from the question that was asked.

The last move is the slowest, and it is the one that does the damage. The small corrections come one at a time: this was Tuesday, not Wednesday; she was not there; that was in the group chat, not in private. Each one is small enough to be an honest mistake. The count is what makes the account disappear. The result is **manufactured doubt**: the reader stops checking the facts and starts checking themselves, and starts asking not *what happened* but *can I be sure I remember it at all*.
examples: The words in the room were not the words in the message; that was revisionism.
The answer moved away from the question about the money; that was deflection.
After the small corrections, the reader began to check his own memory instead of the facts.
sections.heading: How a shared account is rewritten

terms.example: The word was changed from late to careless, and that was revisionism.
terms.gloss: Keeping the account but changing the words in it, until the meaning that was shared is gone.

terms.example: The result was manufactured doubt: he began to check his own memory instead of the record.
terms.gloss: The doubt a person is given about their own memory, until they check themselves instead of the facts.

sections.body:
DARVO is the name of a pattern that often comes with gaslighting. The name is an acronym of its three moves: **deny**, **attack**, and **reverse victim and offender**. Some people use the name for the whole pattern and others use it only for the order of the three moves; both readings are in use, and this article uses the second one.

The three words are plain. A **denial** is the refusal to accept the shared account. The **attack** is the move that turns on the person who holds it: *you are crazy*, *you are just being defensive*, *everyone agrees with me*. The **reverse** puts the two sides in the wrong places: the person who did the harm becomes the one who was hurt, and the person who was harmed is told they are the aggressor. The reversal is the move that makes the pattern hardest to name, because after it the reader is defending themselves against an accusation that the facts have already answered.

Three more words travel with the pattern. **Projection** is putting your own act on the other person: *you are the one who is aggressive*, said by the person who was. **Triangulation** is bringing a third person into a dispute between two: *my sister says I am wrong*, said to the sister, who was not there. The third person carries the claim away from the two people who can actually answer it. **Deflection** is the answer that moves away from the question that was asked.

The English of the pattern is short, and you will hear it at work and at home in the same form. It is a small set of sentences: *you are misremembering*, *I never said that*, *everyone thinks I am the reasonable one here*, *why are you so defensive?* At work it arrives in a review, a handover, or a meeting about what was agreed. At home it arrives after an argument, in a family, or in a group chat where everybody can read it. That set of sentences is the **gaslighting vocabulary**; knowing it is what lets you answer it in the same calm register.
examples: DARVO: deny, attack, and reverse victim and offender.
Triangulation puts a third person into a dispute between two.
Projection puts the actor's own act on the other person.
sections.heading: The words of the subject

terms.example: The pattern was DARVO: deny, attack, and reverse victim and offender.
terms.gloss: The name of the pattern of three moves: deny, attack, and reverse victim and offender.

terms.example: The denial was said the same way every time, and the message did not change it.
terms.gloss: The refusal to accept a shared account, said in a way that does not change when the evidence appears.

terms.example: The attack moved the talk from the handover to her tone.
terms.gloss: The move that turns on the person who holds the account, so that the person becomes the problem.

terms.example: The reversal put the person who caused the harm in the place of the person who suffered it.
terms.gloss: The move that puts the two sides in the wrong places, crediting the harm to the person who suffered it.

terms.example: The answer deflected from the money and went to the tone of the question.
terms.gloss: An answer that moves away from the question that was asked.

terms.example: It was projection: the person who had been aggressive called the other one aggressive.
terms.gloss: Putting your own act on the other person, and calling it the other person's character.

terms.example: Triangulation brought a third person into a dispute between two people.
terms.gloss: Bringing a third person into a dispute between two, so that the two cannot settle it themselves.

terms.example: The gaslighting vocabulary is short: you are misremembering, I never said that.
terms.gloss: The small set of fixed sentences used to rewrite an account, at work and at home.

sections.body:
The three moves are easiest to read as a sequence, but any one of them can be used on its own. The first move removes the account. The second turns on the person who holds it. The third puts the two sides in the wrong places. Each row gives the move three things: what it looks like, what it aims at, and the sentence that answers it.

The last column is the part to keep. In the middle of an argument nobody remembers the definition; people remember the sentence that came ready. Write the three answers on paper and keep them where you can reach them. A move that is answered once and then ignored is not answered: the answer has to be repeated in the same calm voice, and the account has to be brought back each time by the message, the date or the minutes.
examples: The move was the denial, and the answer was the message.
The answer brought the account back instead of arguing about the character.
sections.heading: The three moves of DARVO

rows: "That never happened." "I never said that." "You are misremembering." The sentence is said the same way every time and does not change when the evidence appears.
The account itself. It wants the reader to stop holding a version of events.
"Here is the message from Tuesday, at 14:10. Let us read it together."
"You are crazy." "You are just being defensive." "Everyone agrees with me."
The person who holds the account. It wants the reader treated as the problem, so that the account stops being discussed.
"Let us stay with what happened, and not with what I am like."
"I am the one being hurt here." "You are the aggressive one in this family."
The blame. It wants the harm credited to the person who suffered it, and the person who caused it set free.
"The change was made on Tuesday by your colleague, and the log says so."

sections.body:
Five steps, in order. They work in the middle of a conversation and in the days after it, and they need no special language. The order matters: the record comes before the witness, because a witness asked after the record is usually a witness asked about a version.

The first step keeps the conversation on the subject, so that the account is not lost while the two sides talk about character. The second step is **documentation**: a date, a time, the words used, the people present, the message, the note, the minute of the meeting. The record is the account, and the record survives a denial that memory cannot survive. The third step puts the question to somebody who was there. The fourth step is the boundary, and a boundary that is not kept is only a request. The fifth step is the one nobody skips: what you want from this relationship or this job, what the pattern costs you, and what you are willing to accept, decided while you can still choose.
examples: We are arguing about the handover, not about my character.
Here is the message from Tuesday. Let us read it together.
I will bring the minutes, and we will use them.
sections.heading: What to do when it happens
steps: Name the moment. Say out loud what was said and what is being asked of you: "We are arguing about Tuesday's handover, not about my character."

Keep a record. Write down the date, the time, the words used and who was present: a message, a mail, a handover note, the minute of a meeting. The record is the account, and the record survives the denial.
Look for a witness. Name the person who was there and ask them, not the person who denies, what they saw or heard.
Set the boundary. Say what you will do next time: "If we discuss this, I will bring the minutes and we will use them." Then keep it. A boundary that is not kept is only a request.
Decide what you are staying for. Work out what you want from this relationship or this job, what the pattern costs you, and what you will accept. Decide it while you can still choose.

terms.example: The documentation was a handover note, a date and a message.
terms.gloss: The written record that keeps a shared account alive when memory is attacked.

sections.body:
This article explains a way of speaking. It does not diagnose anybody, and it does not make every disagreement a manipulation. Some people doubt themselves because they are tired, or because they are wrong, or because they were told so for years and never had a reason to check. Doubt is a feeling, and a feeling is not proof of anything.

It does not turn a pattern into a verdict on a person either. A gaslighter is a word for an act, not for a character. People described this way are not all the same, and the description does not tell you what they will do next. Where the pattern is severe, where there is fear or harm, the answer is not a better argument but support: a friend, a doctor, a lawyer, or a service that knows this work.

And it does not replace your own check. The question stays yours: does this conversation move the shared account forward, or does it move it away from what the evidence says?
examples: Doubt is a feeling; it is not proof of a pattern.
The label describes an act, not the worth of the person.
I am still the one who checks the account.
sections.heading: What this article does not do

sections.body:
Use these at the moment you have to decide. The first group is for work, the second for a partner, the third for a family member, and the last for writing, where nobody can interrupt you and the record matters most.

None of them needs a dramatic voice. The point is to hold the account in place with plain words, so that the other person has to answer the facts instead of your character.
examples: Here is the message from Tuesday, at 14:10. Let us read it together.
I am willing to discuss what was said, if we use the minutes.
I remember the evening differently, and I am not going to agree that I do not.
I am not going to talk about my character. I am going to talk about what happened.
My brother says I am wrong, but my brother was not there.
We can talk about the money on Friday, and not about who is the worse person.
To confirm what we agreed: the handover was on Tuesday, at 14:10. My note and the message say the same thing.
I am writing this down so that we have one version of it, not two.
sections.heading: Sentences you can use

sections.body:
The pattern needs a shared account, so it needs two people who remember something together. That is why it appears in the places where people share a life and a memory: a relationship, a family, a team, a department. It appears where one person holds the record: the person who keeps the notes, the one who writes the minutes, the one who remembers the shifts.

A group chat makes it easier. The denial can be written, edited and sent without a face in front of it, and every other person in the chat can read it. The reader is not answering one person any more; the reader is answering a room. A written denial also has a surface the reader can check: a message can be quoted back, and a screenshot is not a memory that can be talked out of. The written form is often where the reader first gets the proof, and often where the audience for it first appears.

An organisation that tolerates the pattern does not have to commit it. It only has to leave it alone. When a complaint about a rewritten account goes nowhere, the message that reaches the people inside is the one the pattern sends: your account is not reliable, and complaining about it is the problem. The cost lands on the people who keep records and speak up, because they are read as difficult, as the source of the conflict, as the person who cannot let things go.

So a group has to make one thing safe: the record. Meetings with minutes, decisions in writing, an answer to a complaint that is about the facts and not about the tone of the person who asked. A group that does this has not solved the pattern; it has stopped the pattern from being invisible, which is the most a group can do by itself.
examples: The meeting had minutes, so the account was in writing.
The complaint was answered on the facts, not on the tone of the person who raised it.
The chat made the denial public, and the screenshot made it checkable.
sections.heading: Where the pattern lives

item.summary: Gaslighting is the rewriting of a shared account until the person who was there doubts their own memory. After reading this you can tell a deliberate attack apart from an ordinary disagreement and an honest mistake, name the three moves of DARVO, recognise the pattern in plain language at work and at home, and answer it with sentences you can reuse.
item.title: Gaslighting and DARVO: Manipulating Perception and Turning the Blame Around
